points: The new account BG 5678-9012 is only 24 days old (account_registry age check) — freshly-opened accounts are a classic vector for supplier-impersonation fraud, where attackers register a company-lookalike account shortly before phishing a bank-change request. The lack of a registry risk flag is not exculpatory; risk flags lag real-world abuse.

Zero payment history to the new account (payment_history) versus 12 clean payments to the old one. There is no established trust with BG 5678-9012 — every safeguard we have is based on the old account. Approving this payment means trusting a channel that has never been validated by a completed, undisputed transaction.

The bolagsverket SNI code check shows a mismatch: the company is named 'Kontorsmaterial' (office supplies) but is registered under SNI 43.999 (specialised construction). That is exactly the sort of inconsistency you see when a shell or hijacked entity is being used — or when the orgnr being cited does not actually correspond to the trading name on the invoice. This deserves escalation, not dismissal as 'unrelated'.

The web_intel 'announcement' on the supplier's website is weak corroboration: websites are routinely compromised or spoofed in BEC attacks, and the fact that it 'matches the invoice's raw_note' is circular — an attacker who controls the invoice text can also plant or alter a matching web notice. points: The advocate's 'two independent sources' are not actually independent. The account_registry confirms only that BG 5678-9012 belongs to orgnr 556234-1122 — but that same orgnr could have been compromised (credential theft, insider, or takeover of the SEB banking relationship). Registry ownership does not prove the CHANGE request is authorized by the legitimate controllers of the business; it only proves the destination account is nominally under the same orgnr umbrella. In sophisticated supplier-takeover fraud, attackers open a NEW account at a NEW bank (note: SEB is new — we have no evidence the supplier previously banked at SEB) under the real orgnr, precisely so ownership checks pass.

The website announcement and the invoice raw_note are also NOT independent channels — both are attacker-controllable in a supplier-compromise scenario. If the fraudster has taken over the supplier's email (faktura@sveakontor.se would then still 'match' — point 3 of the advocate collapses), they almost certainly have or can obtain website CMS access, or the announcement itself could have been posted by a compromised insider. Matching content across attacker-reachable surfaces is expected in BEC, not exculpatory.

The 24-day account age plus a bank MIGRATION (from the old BG provider to SEB) is a compounding signal, not a single one. The registry 'did not flag' it because registries flag known-bad accounts, not newly-opened-and-not-yet-abused ones. Combined with zero payment history to the new account, we have literally no independent transactional evidence that this account behaves as the supplier's operating account.

The advocate dismisses the SNI mismatch, but 43.999 (specialised construction) for an 'office supplies' trading name is exactly the kind of anomaly that warrants — at minimum — the 10-minute phone callback that would resolve this entire dispute. The advocate has offered no reason NOT to do the callback, only reasons the paper trail looks fine.

Asymmetric cost analysis still favors holding: a 24–48 hour delay for out-of-band voice verification to a pre-existing supplier phone number costs essentially nothing (the supplier's own announcement grants a grace period until 30 September). Approving on paper evidence alone, if wrong, loses 15,100 SEK AND establishes BG 5678-9012 as a 'trusted' channel for the next, larger fraudulent invoice.
